# Cold-Chain Storage

Temperature-sensitive products are stored between 2 °C and 8 °C.
Any excursion above 8 °C for more than 30 minutes is a deviation, see [[sop-deviation]].
Temperature loggers are read before a cold-chain lot is released, see [[sop-lot-release]].

# Warehouse Storage

Room-temperature products are stored between 15 °C and 25 °C with relative humidity below 60%.
Refrigerated products are stored per [[sop-cold-chain]].

Warehouse locations are mapped for temperature every 2 years and after any change to the building or HVAC system.
QUARANTINE, REJECTED, and RECALLED stock is kept in a physically separate, locked area. Only warehouse staff with the quarantine role can move stock in or out of it.

A full stock count is done once a year. A count difference above 0.5% for any SKU is investigated as a deviation, see [[sop-deviation]].

# Stability Testing

Stability studies confirm a product stays within specification for its full shelf life.

The first three commercial lots of every new product enter the stability program. After that, one lot per SKU per year is added.
Long-term samples are tested at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months, then yearly until the end of shelf life.
Refrigerated products are stored at 5 °C ± 3 °C for long-term testing. Room-temperature products are stored at 25 °C ± 2 °C and 60% relative humidity.

A stability result outside specification is an out-of-specification result, see [[sop-oos]], and is reported to the Head of Quality within 2 working days.
Shelf life can only be extended after real-time data covers the new period, and the extension is a change under [[sop-change-control]].

Returned product is placed in QUARANTINE on arrival and is never put straight back into saleable stock.

Returned goods can be returned to stock only if all of these are true: the packaging is unopened, the product stayed within its storage conditions the whole time, and more than 12 months of shelf life remain.

response: Returned product is placed in **QUARANTINE** on arrival. It is never put straight back into saleable stock.

question: What temperature and humidity are room-temperature products stored at?
reference_answer: Between 15 °C and 25 °C, with relative humidity below 60%.

# Warehouse Storage

Room-temperature products are stored between 15 °C and 25 °C with relative humidity below 60%.
Refrigerated products are stored per [[sop-cold-chain]].

Warehouse locations are mapped for temperature every 2 years and after any change to the building or HVAC system.
QUARANTINE, REJECTED, and RECALLED stock is kept in a physically separate, locked area. Only warehouse staff with the quarantine role can move stock in or out of it.

A full stock count is done once a year. A count difference above 0.5% for any SKU is investigated as a deviation, see [[sop-deviation]].

# Stability Testing

Stability studies confirm a product stays within specification for its full shelf life.

The first three commercial lots of every new product enter the stability program. After that, one lot per SKU per year is added.
Long-term samples are tested at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months, then yearly until the end of shelf life.
Refrigerated products are stored at 5 °C ± 3 °C for long-term testing. Room-temperature products are stored at 25 °C ± 2 °C and 60% relative humidity.

A stability result outside specification is an out-of-specification result, see [[sop-oos]], and is reported to the Head of Quality within 2 working days.
Shelf life can only be extended after real-time data covers the new period, and the extension is a change under [[sop-change-control]].

# Cold-Chain Storage

Temperature-sensitive products are stored between 2 °C and 8 °C.
Any excursion above 8 °C for more than 30 minutes is a deviation, see [[sop-deviation]].
Temperature loggers are read before a cold-chain lot is released, see [[sop-lot-release]].

SKU-099 (Cardiolex 5 mg injection) is refrigerated, stored between 2 °C and 8 °C, with a shelf life of 18 months.
SKU-120 (Dermasol cream 50 g) is shelf-stable at room temperature, with a shelf life of 36 months.
SKU-145 (Pulmovent inhaler) is stored at room temperature, with a shelf life of 24 months.
SKU-210 (Glycobal 500 mg tablets) is stored at room temperature, with a shelf life of 48 months.
SKU-305 (Vaxigen vaccine 0.5 mL) is refrigerated and must never be frozen, with a shelf life of 12 months.

Refrigerated SKUs follow [[sop-cold-chain]]. Room-temperature SKUs follow [[sop-warehouse-storage]].
SKU-077 was discontinued in 2024; its number is kept and never reassigned, see [[catalog-sku]].

# Record Retention

Batch records and QA sign-off records are kept for 1 year after the lot's expiry date, or 5 years after release, whichever is longer.
Shipping and distribution records are kept for 5 years.
Training records are kept for the length of employment plus 10 years.
Complaint and recall records are kept for 10 years.

Records may be destroyed only after the retention period ends and QA approves the destruction list.
Records under a legal hold are never destroyed, whatever their retention period.
Electronic records must stay readable for the whole retention period, including after a system is retired.

# Shipping and Distribution

Only lots with status RELEASED can be shipped. A lot on HOLD, in QUARANTINE, or RECALLED is blocked by the warehouse system.

Orders are picked first-expiry, first-out (FEFO). A lot with less than 6 months of remaining shelf life is not shipped unless the customer agrees in writing.
Cold-chain shipments use validated insulated shippers with a temperature logger in each shipper, and must arrive within 48 hours, see [[sop-cold-chain]].

Each shipment record stores the lot number, customer, quantity, and dispatch date. These records support the 4-hour trace in [[sop-recall]] and are kept per [[policy-record-retention]].

A recall removes distributed product from the market. It is decided by the Recall Committee, chaired by the Head of Quality.

Recall classes: Class I (risk of serious harm or death), Class II (risk of temporary or reversible harm), Class III (unlikely to cause harm).
The regulator is notified within 24 hours for a Class I recall and within 72 hours for Class II and Class III.

Distribution records must allow every customer who received the lot to be identified within 4 hours, see [[sop-shipping]].
Initiating a recall changes lot status to RECALLED and is a Tier 3 action, see [[policy-hitl-approval]].
A mock recall is run once a year for one randomly chosen lot to test the 4-hour trace.

question: A lot's batch record review is complete and all in-process checks are within limits, but QA has not signed off yet. Can the lot be released?

# QA Sign-Off

QA sign-off is step 4 of lot release, see [[sop-lot-release]]. Only a Qualified Person (QP) may sign off a lot.

Before signing, the QP confirms that the batch record review is complete, all in-process checks are within limits, there are no open deviations against the lot, and, for cold-chain lots, the temperature log is acceptable.
The sign-off is recorded in the state store with the QP's user ID and a timestamp. It is a Tier 3 action and goes through [[policy-hitl-approval]].

A QP may not sign off a lot they personally manufactured or reviewed in production.
A sign-off can be revoked only by the Head of Quality. Revoking a sign-off puts the lot on HOLD.

# Lot Release Safety Protocol

Every production lot (format LOT-NNNNN) must pass a safety verification before release.
Verification requires: (1) batch record review complete, (2) all in-process checks within limits,
(3) no open deviations against the lot, and (4) QA sign-off recorded in the state store.

A lot in status HOLD cannot be shipped. Releasing a lot is a Tier 3 mutation and requires
reviewer approval, see [[policy-hitl-approval]]. Open deviations are handled per [[sop-deviation]].
Cold-chain lots also need a temperature log check, see [[sop-cold-chain]].

# Batch Record Review

Every lot has an executed batch record (EBR). The batch record review is step 1 of lot release, see [[sop-lot-release]].

Production reviews the EBR first, within 2 working days of the end of manufacture. QA then performs an independent second review.
The reviewer checks that every step is signed and dated, every recorded value is within its limit, and every correction follows [[policy-data-integrity]].

Missing signatures, unexplained gaps, or values outside limits are review findings. A finding that cannot be explained by documentation is raised as a deviation, see [[sop-deviation]].
The review is complete only when all findings are closed and QA has signed the review page.
Target cycle time from end of manufacture to completed review is 5 working days.

# In-Process Checks

In-process checks (IPCs) confirm a lot stays within limits while it is being made. All IPC results are step 2 of lot release, see [[sop-lot-release]].

Standard IPCs for tablets: weight every 15 minutes, hardness every 30 minutes, and disintegration once per hour.
Standard IPCs for liquids: pH and fill volume every 20 minutes.

A single result outside limits stops the line. The operator retests once with a fresh sample. If the retest is also outside limits, the shift supervisor raises a deviation, see [[sop-deviation]].
An IPC instrument must have a valid calibration on the day of use, see [[sop-calibration]]. Results from an instrument found out of calibration are invalid back to its last passing calibration.

Any action that changes records (lot release, status change, form submission) is Tier 3.
The assistant never executes Tier 3 actions itself. It creates a PENDING_APPROVAL request and

System actions are grouped into three tiers.
TIER_1_READ: read records and search the knowledge base.
TIER_2_COMPUTE: run calculations and reports that do not change records.
TIER_3_MUTATE: change records, such as lot release, status changes, and form submission. Tier 3 always needs human approval, see [[policy-hitl-approval]].

Access is granted by role, never per person. Role assignments are reviewed every quarter by each department head.
Accounts are disabled within 24 hours of a person leaving the company. Accounts unused for 90 days are disabled automatically.
Every request carries a tenant ID, and a user can only see data for their own tenant.

A recall removes distributed product from the market. It is decided by the Recall Committee, chaired by the Head of Quality.

Recall classes: Class I (risk of serious harm or death), Class II (risk of temporary or reversible harm), Class III (unlikely to cause harm).
The regulator is notified within 24 hours for a Class I recall and within 72 hours for Class II and Class III.

Distribution records must allow every customer who received the lot to be identified within 4 hours, see [[sop-shipping]].
Initiating a recall changes lot status to RECALLED and is a Tier 3 action, see [[policy-hitl-approval]].
A mock recall is run once a year for one randomly chosen lot to test the 4-hour trace.

The assistant answers questions from the approved knowledge base and helps prepare records. It cites the notes it used.

# Root-Cause Analysis

Root-cause analysis (RCA) is required for every Major and Critical deviation and every confirmed out-of-specification result, see [[sop-oos]].
The RCA report is due within 15 working days of deviation classification.

Approved methods are the 5 Whys, the fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, and fault-tree analysis. Critical deviations must use at least two methods.

An out-of-specification (OOS) result is a test result outside its approved specification.

Phase I is a laboratory investigation by the analyst and the lab supervisor, completed within 3 working days. It checks for calculation errors, instrument problems, and sample preparation errors.

Cold-chain shipments use validated insulated shippers with a temperature logger in each shipper, and must arrive within 48 hours, see [[sop-cold-chain]].

Each shipment record stores the lot number, customer, quantity, and dispatch date. These records support the 4-hour trace in [[sop-recall]] and are kept per [[policy-record-retention]].

# Returned Goods

Returned product is placed in QUARANTINE on arrival and is never put straight back into saleable stock.

Returned goods can be returned to stock only if all of these are true: the packaging is unopened, the product stayed within its storage conditions the whole time, and more than 12 months of shelf life remain.
Cold-chain products can never be returned to stock, because their storage history outside our control cannot be verified. They are destroyed.

The decision to return to stock is made by QA and recorded against the original lot number.
Product returned because of a complaint is handled under [[sop-complaint-handling]] and kept as evidence until that complaint is closed.

# Incoming Material Inspection

Every incoming delivery is placed in QUARANTINE on receipt and cannot be used until QC releases it.

QC checks the delivery against the purchase order, the supplier's certificate of analysis, and the label. Active ingredients are identity-tested on every container.
Other materials from approved suppliers are sampled using the square-root rule: sample √n + 1 containers, where n is the number of containers delivered.
Materials from a supplier on conditional status are fully tested, see [[sop-supplier-qualification]].

Released material gets a green RELEASED label. Rejected material gets a red REJECTED label and is returned or destroyed within 30 days.
Cold-chain materials are checked for temperature excursions during transport before they are moved into storage, see [[sop-cold-chain]].

# Lot Numbering

Lot numbers use the format LOT-NNNNN: the prefix LOT-, then exactly five digits, zero padded. For example, lot 44 is written LOT-00044.

Lot numbers are assigned in sequence by the manufacturing system when the batch record is opened, and are never reused, even if the lot is rejected.
One lot is made from one SKU on one line in one continuous run. A lot that is split for packaging keeps its lot number, with suffixes -A, -B, and so on for each split.
The lot status lifecycle is: QUARANTINE → RELEASED, or QUARANTINE → REJECTED. A released lot can later move to HOLD or RECALLED. See [[sop-lot-release]].
SKU formats are defined in [[catalog-sku]].

# Root-Cause Analysis

Root-cause analysis (RCA) is required for every Major and Critical deviation and every confirmed out-of-specification result, see [[sop-oos]].
The RCA report is due within 15 working days of deviation classification.

Approved methods are the 5 Whys, the fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, and fault-tree analysis. Critical deviations must use at least two methods.
The RCA team includes the process owner, a QA representative, and at least one operator from the affected shift.

"Human error" is not accepted as a root cause on its own. The report must state why the error was possible, for example unclear instructions or missing training, see [[sop-training]].
When no root cause can be found, the report is labelled "root cause not determined" and the CAPA must include extra monitoring for 6 months, see [[sop-capa]].

# Stability Testing

Stability studies confirm a product stays within specification for its full shelf life.

The first three commercial lots of every new product enter the stability program. After that, one lot per SKU per year is added.
Long-term samples are tested at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months, then yearly until the end of shelf life.
Refrigerated products are stored at 5 °C ± 3 °C for long-term testing. Room-temperature products are stored at 25 °C ± 2 °C and 60% relative humidity.

A stability result outside specification is an out-of-specification result, see [[sop-oos]], and is reported to the Head of Quality within 2 working days.
Shelf life can only be extended after real-time data covers the new period, and the extension is a change under [[sop-change-control]].
